description: Comparison tools and decision guidance for menopause treatment options

entries.title: HRT Types Comparison: Delivery Methods
entries.description: Comparing oral, transdermal, and vaginal estrogen delivery
entries.content: Different HRT delivery methods have different benefits, risks, and convenience factors. The best choice depends on your symptoms, risk factors, and preferences.

pros: Good for hot flashes and systemic symptoms
cons: Higher risk of blood clots than transdermal
First-pass liver metabolism (may affect some women)
Not ideal if history of blood clots or migraines
comparison_table.best_for: Women without blood clot risk, prefer pills, need systemic symptom relief
comparison_table.avoid_if: History of blood clots, stroke, migraines with aura, liver disease

pros: Lower blood clot risk than oral
Good for migraines, blood clot concerns
cons: May not stick well with sweating/swimming
comparison_table.best_for: Women with blood clot risk, migraines, liver concerns, prefer less frequent dosing
comparison_table.avoid_if: Severe skin sensitivity, allergies to adhesives

forms: Daily gel or spray applied to skin
pros: Lower blood clot risk than oral
Good for skin-sensitive women who can't use patches
cons: Must let dry before contact with others (especially children/pets)
Can transfer to others before dry
comparison_table.best_for: Women who want transdermal benefits without patch visibility, can't tolerate patches
comparison_table.avoid_if: Close contact with children/pets immediately after application difficult to avoid

forms: Cream, tablet, or ring inserted vaginally
pros: Safe for many women who can't take systemic HRT
cons: Doesn't help hot flashes, mood, bones
comparison_table.best_for: Women with only vaginal/urinary symptoms, or those who can't take systemic HRT
comparison_table.avoid_if: Need treatment for hot flashes or other systemic symptoms (would need additional treatment)

entries.progesterone_note: If you have a uterus, you need progesterone with systemic estrogen to protect uterine lining. Progesterone comes as: oral pill (often causes drowsiness - take at night), IUD (Mirena), or combined estrogen-progesterone patch.

entries.title: HRT vs Non-Hormonal Treatments Decision Guide
entries.description: When to choose hormonal vs non-hormonal options
entries.content: Both hormonal and non-hormonal treatments have roles in menopause management. The choice depends on symptom severity, risk factors, and personal preferences.

decision_factors.choose_HRT_if: Moderate to severe symptoms significantly affecting quality of life; multiple symptoms
decision_factors.choose_non_hormonal_if: Mild symptoms; only one or two bothersome symptoms
decision_factors.rationale: HRT is most effective for multiple moderate-severe symptoms; non-hormonal may suffice for mild cases

decision_factors.choose_HRT_if: Under 60 or within 10 years of menopause; early/premature menopause
decision_factors.choose_non_hormonal_if: Over 60 or more than 10 years past menopause (higher HRT risks)
decision_factors.rationale: HRT benefits outweigh risks when started early; risks increase with later start

decision_factors.choose_HRT_if: No contraindications; family history of osteoporosis; need bone protection
decision_factors.choose_non_hormonal_if: History of blood clots, stroke, breast cancer, or other contraindications
decision_factors.rationale: Some conditions make HRT unsafe; non-hormonal options are safer alternatives

decision_factors.choose_HRT_if: Hot flashes, night sweats, vaginal dryness, mood issues, joint pain, bone loss concerns
decision_factors.choose_non_hormonal_if: Primarily hot flashes only, or can't/won't take hormones
decision_factors.rationale: HRT treats widest range of symptoms; some non-hormonal options target specific symptoms

decision_factors.choose_HRT_if: Comfortable with hormones; want most effective option; willing to accept small risks
decision_factors.choose_non_hormonal_if: Prefer to avoid hormones; concerned about HRT risks; want 'natural' approach
decision_factors.rationale: Personal values and comfort matter; both approaches have evidence

entries.combination_approach: Many women use both: HRT for systemic symptoms + lifestyle changes + CBT for coping. This isn't either/or.
entries.can_switch: You can start with non-hormonal and switch to HRT later if needed, or vice versa. Treatment can be adjusted.

entries.title: HRT Risk Assessment Guidance
entries.description: Understanding and evaluating your individual HRT risks
entries.content: HRT risks are individual and depend on age, timing, type of HRT, duration, and personal/family history. Absolute risks are generally small for most women under 60.

risk_categories.absolute_risk: Combined HRT: ~1 extra case per 1,000 women per year. Estrogen-only: no increased risk or slight decrease.
risk_categories.context: Similar risk to drinking 2 glasses of wine daily or being overweight. Risk decreases after stopping.

risk_categories.absolute_risk: Oral estrogen: ~2 extra cases per 1,000 women per year. Transdermal: minimal to no increased risk.
risk_categories.context: Transdermal estrogen avoids this risk. Pregnancy carries higher VTE risk than HRT.

risk_categories.absolute_risk: Small increase with oral estrogen, especially if started after 60. Transdermal may be safer.
risk_categories.context: Risk is age-dependent. Very low for women under 60 with controlled blood pressure.

risk_categories.absolute_risk: DECREASED risk if started within 10 years of menopause. Increased risk if started >10 years after.
risk_categories.context: Timing is everything. Early HRT may protect heart; late HRT may increase risk.

benefits_to_weigh: Possible heart disease prevention if started early
entries.individual_assessment: Your doctor should assess YOUR specific risks based on age, timing, medical history, family history, and type of HRT. Risks are not one-size-fits-all.

entries.title: Treatment Effectiveness Comparison
entries.description: How effective are different treatments for specific symptoms
entries.content: Different treatments have different effectiveness levels for various symptoms. This helps set realistic expectations.

effectiveness_by_symptom.lifestyle_helps: Cooling strategies, avoiding triggers, stress management - helps coping, doesn't eliminate

limited_effectiveness: Oral HRT - helps but less than local estrogen
effectiveness_by_symptom.lifestyle_helps: Regular sexual activity, moisturizers, adequate hydration
Exercise, stress management, sleep hygiene, mindfulness - significant impact

effectiveness_by_symptom.most_effective: HRT (if due to night sweats) - 70-80% improvement
limited_effectiveness: Sleep aids alone without addressing cause - temporary
effectiveness_by_symptom.lifestyle_helps: Sleep hygiene, cool bedroom, stress management - essential foundation

moderately_effective: Calcium + Vitamin D + weight-bearing exercise - 40-50% prevention
limited_effectiveness: Exercise alone - helps but not enough
effectiveness_by_symptom.lifestyle_helps: Weight-bearing exercise, resistance training, adequate calcium/vitamin D - essential

entries.combination_note: Combining treatments (e.g., HRT + lifestyle + CBT) often works better than single approach.

entries.title: Bioidentical vs Synthetic Hormones
entries.description: Understanding the terminology and actual differences
entries.content: There's confusion about 'bioidentical' vs 'synthetic' hormones. The truth is more nuanced than marketing suggests.

terminology_clarification.body_identical: Chemically identical to hormones your body makes. Includes FDA-approved estradiol and micronized progesterone.
terminology_clarification.bioidentical: Marketing term often used for compounded hormones, but also applies to FDA-approved body-identical hormones.
terminology_clarification.synthetic: Chemically different from body's hormones (like conjugated equine estrogens from horse urine, or progestins like medroxyprogesterone).

comparison.source: Plant-derived (soy/yam) but synthesized in lab to match human hormones
comparison.regulation: FDA-approved, tested for purity, consistent dosing
comparison.safety_profile: Well-studied; micronized progesterone may have better safety than synthetic progestins

comparison.source: Same plant-derived hormones, custom-mixed by compounding pharmacy
comparison.regulation: NOT FDA-approved, no quality control testing
comparison.safety_profile: Same risks as regulated hormones but without quality oversight; batch-to-batch variation
comparison.cost: Often NOT covered by insurance, expensive
comparison.recommendation: NOT RECOMMENDED except for allergies or unique needs

comparison.source: Conjugated equine estrogens (horse urine) or synthetic progestins
comparison.safety_profile: Well-studied; some synthetic progestins may have slightly higher risks than micronized progesterone
comparison.cost: Usually covered by insurance, often generic
comparison.recommendation: Acceptable option, though body-identical often preferred

entries.bottom_line: FDA-approved body-identical hormones (estradiol, micronized progesterone) are the best choice: they're bioidentical, regulated, safe, and effective. Compounded hormones are not recommended.
